response:
Given your exclusions, the most likely remaining source is inside Docker Desktop’s WSL main VM disk, not daemon.json, not the Windows registry, not Docker context, and not the installer binary.
For Docker Desktop WSL2, Docker’s WSL backend stores its Linux VM data under:
PowerShell%LOCALAPPDATA%\Docker\wsl
Docker documents this as the WSL2 backend data location, and recent Docker Desktop versions have moved away from the old separate docker-desktop-data distro toward VHDX files under this tree. Community reports for newer Docker Desktop builds specifically mention main\ext4.vhdx and data VHDX files under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Docker\wsl. Microsoft Learn Docker Community Forums
The exact setting Docker Desktop materializes into:
PowerShell%USERPROFILE%\.docker\daemon.json
is its internal linuxDockerdConfiguration object. Docker Desktop diagnostics show the settings loader merging providers and ending with a settings state containing:
JSON"linuxDockerdConfiguration": { ... }
and Docker’s own settings docs confirm the Desktop Docker Engine JSON lives at $HOME/.docker/daemon.json. GitHub Docker Documentation
So in your case, with every host-side provider clean, inspect:
PowerShell%LOCALAPPDATA%\Docker\wsl\main\ext4.vhdx
not primarily:
PowerShell%LOCALAPPDATA%\Docker\wsl\data\docker_data.vhdx
docker_data.vhdx is more likely the Docker data disk; the daemon configuration source is more likely in the main VM disk.

Check the VHDX directly
Run PowerShell as Administrator:
PowerShell# Stop Docker and WSL completelyStop-Process -Name "Docker Desktop" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueStop-Process -Name "com.docker.backend" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueStop-Process -Name "com.docker.proxy" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueStop-Process -Name "com.docker.service" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinuewsl --shutdown# Find Docker Desktop VHDX filesGet-ChildItem "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Docker\wsl" -Recurse -Filter *.vhdx | Select-Object FullName, Length
Now mount the likely main VM disk:
PowerShell$mainVhd = Get-ChildItem "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Docker\wsl" -Recurse -Filter ext4.vhdx | Sort-Object Length | Select-Object -First 1Write-Host "Mounting $($mainVhd.FullName)"wsl --mount "$($mainVhd.FullName)" --vhd --bare
Find the new block device from any WSL distro:
PowerShellwsl --exec sh -lc "lsblk -f"
Look for the newly attached ext4 disk, usually /dev/sdX.
Then mount it read-only and grep:
PowerShellwsl --exec sh -lc "sudo mkdir -p /mnt/docker-desktop-main"# Replace /dev/sdX with the actual device from lsblkwsl --exec sh -lc "sudo mount -o ro /dev/sdX /mnt/docker-desktop-main"wsl --exec sh -lc "sudo grep -RIn --binary-files=text -E 'D:\\\\Code\\\\docker-data|D:/Code/docker-data|data-root|linuxDockerdConfiguration' /mnt/docker-desktop-main 2>/dev/null"
The file you are looking for is most likely one of these inside the mounted VHDX:
/mnt/docker-desktop-main/etc/docker/daemon.json/mnt/docker-desktop-main/run/config/docker/daemon.json/mnt/docker-desktop-main/var/config/docker/daemon.json/mnt/docker-desktop-main/etc/docker/daemon.d/*
When done:
PowerShellwsl --exec sh -lc "sudo umount /mnt/docker-desktop-main"wsl --unmount

If found inside main\ext4.vhdx
The cleanest permanent reset is to remove Docker Desktop’s WSL disks and the regenerated host daemon file:
PowerShellStop-Process -Name "Docker Desktop" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueStop-Process -Name "com.docker.backend" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueStop-Process -Name "com.docker.proxy" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueStop-Process -Name "com.docker.service" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinuewsl --shutdownRemove-Item "$env:USERPROFILE\.docker\daemon.json" -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueRemove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Docker\wsl" -Recurse -ForceStart-Process "C:\Program Files\Docker\Docker\Docker Desktop.exe"
This forces Docker Desktop to recreate fresh WSL backend disks. It will delete local images, containers, volumes, builders, and Kubernetes state.
Then verify:
PowerShelldocker info --format '{{.DockerRootDir}}'Get-Content "$env:USERPROFILE\.docker\daemon.json" -Raw
Expected:
/var/lib/docker
and no:
JSON"data-root": "D:\\Code\\docker-data"

If grep does not find it inside the VHDX
Then the remaining source is not a file you listed; it is one of Docker Desktop’s settings providers writing linuxDockerdConfiguration during startup. Use the settings-loader logs to identify the provider:
PowerShellGet-ChildItem "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Docker" "$env:APPDATA\Docker" -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $_.Length -lt 100MB } | Select-String -Pattern "D:\\Code\\docker-data","data-root","linuxDockerdConfiguration","settingsloader","Source:" -SimpleMatch -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Path, LineNumber, Line
Also explicitly check the two provider files you did not list:
PowerShellGet-Item "$env:APPDATA\Docker\cloud-settings.json" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueGet-Item "$env:APPDATA\Docker\registry.json" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinueSelect-String -Path "$env:APPDATA\Docker\cloud-settings.json","$env:APPDATA\Docker\registry.json" ` -Pattern "D:\\Code\\docker-data","data-root","linuxDockerdConfiguration" ` -SimpleMatch -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Docker Desktop settings management can also come from Admin Console policies, not only local JSON. Docker documents centralized Settings Management through the Admin Console and admin-settings.json; if you are signed in to a Docker Business organization, cloud policy can apply at startup. Docker Documentation Docker

Direct answer to your candidates
CandidateVerdictInside WSL .vhdxYes, now the most likely remaining source. Check main\ext4.vhdx first.docker_data.vhdxPossible but less likely; grep it too only if main\ext4.vhdx is clean.Installer binaryNo. Docker Desktop does not persist user daemon preferences inside the EXE/MSI.Environment variableNo, not for persistent daemon.json recreation.MSI installer databaseNo, especially with clean install-settings.json.Docker context fileNo. Contexts store endpoint metadata; they do not rewrite Docker Engine daemon.json.Cloud/Admin policyPossible if VHDX grep is clean and you are signed in to an org.
The exact thing being persisted is the Docker Desktop setting:
JSON"linuxDockerdConfiguration": { "data-root": "D:\\Code\\docker-data"}
In your fact pattern, the exact place to inspect next is:
PowerShell%LOCALAPPDATA%\Docker\wsl\main\ext4.vhdx
and the practical permanent reset command is:
PowerShellRemove-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Docker\wsl" -Recurse -Force
after fully stopping Docker Desktop and WSL.
